title: Attention is all you need
why: The original paper: scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, sinusoidal positions, the post-norm block and the encoder-decoder layout. Short, and still the right place to start.

title: Improving language understanding by generative pre-training (GPT)
why: The first decoder-only transformer language model trained on next-token prediction and then fine-tuned; the recipe the deck describes. Not on arXiv.

title: Language models are unsupervised multitask learners (GPT-2)
why: GPT-2: the 124M/355M/774M/1.5B family, pre-norm, byte-level BPE, tied embeddings; the configuration the deck counts by hand. The code and configs are at github.com/openai/gpt-2. Not on arXiv.

title: A mathematical framework for transformer circuits
why: The residual-stream view of slide 4: heads as independent read-write operations on a shared stream, QK and OV circuits, and the first analysis of induction heads. Published as a web article, not on arXiv.

title: Formal algorithms for transformers
why: Every component of the deck written out as pseudocode with explicit shapes: tokenization, embeddings, attention, the block, training and decoding. The best companion for checking one's understanding line by line.

title: Neural machine translation by jointly learning to align and translate
why: Where attention came from: a translation decoder that computes a soft alignment over the source positions instead of compressing the sentence into one vector.

title: The illustrated transformer (blog)
why: The most widely read visual walkthrough of the 2017 architecture; the deck's pictures of Q, K, V and multi-head attention follow the same conventions. Secondary source.

title: nanoGPT (code repository)
why: A complete GPT-2 implementation and training loop in about 300 lines of PyTorch; reading model.py after the deck turns every slide into a few lines of code. Secondary source.

title: Neural machine translation of rare words with subword units
why: Byte-pair encoding as a subword vocabulary for neural models; the method behind every tokenizer on slide 5.

title: SentencePiece: a simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for neural text processing
why: The library used by Llama 2 and many others; treats the input as a raw stream, so whitespace is just another symbol.

title: Subword regularization: improving neural network translation models with multiple subword candidates
why: The unigram language-model tokenizer, the main alternative to BPE, and why sampling among segmentations helps training.

title: Scaling laws with vocabulary: larger models deserve larger vocabularies
why: Why vocabularies grew from 32k to 128k-256k: the compute-optimal vocabulary size rises with model size.

title: Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space
why: word2vec: word vectors from context prediction, and the king - man + woman = queen regularity of slide 7.

title: RoFormer: enhanced transformer with rotary position embedding
why: RoPE: rotate queries and keys by position so that attention scores depend only on relative distance; the position scheme of Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma (slide 9).

title: Self-attention with relative position representations
why: The first relative-position scheme for transformers, adding learned offset vectors to keys; the idea RoPE makes parameter-free.

title: Train short, test long: attention with linear biases enables input length extrapolation
why: ALiBi: no position vectors at all, just a distance penalty added to the scores; used by BLOOM and MPT, and the clearest statement of the length-extrapolation problem.

title: Extending context window of large language models via positional interpolation
why: Rescale RoPE angles so that a longer context maps onto the trained range, then fine-tune briefly; the basis of most context extension.

title: YaRN: efficient context window extension of large language models
why: Frequency-aware RoPE rescaling: stretch the slow pairs, leave the fast ones; used by several long-context open models.

title: Effective approaches to attention-based neural machine translation
why: Dot-product scoring between a query state and key states, the scoring function the transformer adopted, compared with alternatives.

title: What does BERT look at? An analysis of BERT's attention
why: Attention heads that track syntactic relations and coreference, and heads that park on [SEP] when idle; the source of slide 16's patterns.

authors: Voita, Talbot, Moiseev, Sennrich and Titov
title: Analyzing multi-head self-attention: specialized heads do the heavy lifting, the rest can be pruned
why: Positional, syntactic and rare-word heads in a translation model, and the finding that most other heads can be removed.

title: In-context learning and induction heads
why: Induction heads as the mechanism of in-context learning in small models, and their appearance as a bend in the training curve.

authors: Xiao, Tian, Chen, Han and Lewis
title: Efficient streaming language models with attention sinks
why: The attention sink: idle attention parks on the first token, and keeping it in the cache is what makes sliding-window generation work.

authors: Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra and Re
title: FlashAttention: fast and memory-efficient exact attention with IO-awareness
why: Exact attention computed in tiles without materializing the T x T matrix; the implementation every model uses (slide 28).

title: FlashAttention-2: faster attention with better parallelism and work partitioning
why: The second version, with the work split that reaches a large fraction of peak on H100s.

title: Transformer feed-forward layers are key-value memories
why: Rows of W1 as pattern detectors and columns of W2 as the updates they write; the reading of the MLP on slide 17.

title: Gaussian error linear units (GELUs)
why: GELU and SiLU, the smooth activations of BERT, GPT-2 and the SwiGLU gate.

title: Searching for activation functions
why: Swish, x times sigmoid(x), found by search and shown to beat ReLU across tasks; the same function as SiLU.

title: Language modeling with gated convolutional networks
why: The gated linear unit: one projection gates another elementwise; the structure SwiGLU inherits.

title: GLU variants improve transformer
why: SwiGLU and its relatives as the transformer MLP, with the 8/3 d hidden width that keeps the parameter count fixed (slide 18).

title: Deep residual learning for image recognition
why: Residual connections: learn a correction and add it to the input, which lets very deep networks train (slide 19).

title: Layer normalization
why: Normalize over the features of one example rather than over a batch; the norm of the 2017 Transformer, BERT and GPT-2.

title: Root mean square layer normalization
why: Drop the centering, keep the scaling: the cheaper norm used by Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma (slide 20).

title: On layer normalization in the transformer architecture
why: Why post-norm needs warm-up and pre-norm does not: the gradient scale at initialization under the two placements (slide 19).

title: BERT rediscovers the classical NLP pipeline
why: Probing shows syntax resolved in earlier layers and semantics later; the division-of-labor note on slide 22.

title: Scale efficiently: insights from pre-training and fine-tuning transformers
why: How depth and width trade off at fixed compute; deeper-narrower tends to win downstream.

title: Using the output embedding to improve language models
why: Weight tying: use the embedding matrix as the unembedding; saves V d parameters and improves perplexity (slide 23).

authors: Holtzman, Buys, Du, Forbes and Choi
title: The curious case of neural text degeneration
why: Why greedy and beam search produce bland, repetitive text, and nucleus (top-p) sampling as the fix (slide 24).

title: Hierarchical neural story generation
why: Top-k sampling, introduced here for story generation.

title: Fast transformer decoding: one write-head is all you need
why: Multi-query attention: share one key/value head across all query heads to shrink the KV cache and speed up decoding.

title: GQA: training generalized multi-query transformer models from multi-head checkpoints
why: Grouped-query attention, the middle ground used by Llama 2 70B and all of Llama 3 (slides 25 and 29).

title: Efficiently scaling transformer inference
why: The cost model of decoding: memory-bound at small batch, the KV cache as the limit, and the partitioning strategies that follow.

title: Efficient memory management for large language model serving with PagedAttention
why: vLLM: manage the KV cache in pages like virtual memory, which is what lets a GPU serve many sequences at once.

title: Fast inference from transformers via speculative decoding
why: Draft several tokens with a small model and verify them in one pass of the large one; exact sampling at a fraction of the decode steps.

title: Decoupled weight decay regularization
why: AdamW, the optimizer used for essentially all LLM training.

title: Scaling laws for neural language models
why: Loss as a power law in parameters, data and compute; the 6ND cost model; and the finding that shape (depth versus width) matters little (slides 22 and 28).

title: Training compute-optimal large language models
why: Chinchilla: about twenty training tokens per parameter at the compute-optimal point; why current models train on trillions of tokens.

title: Megatron-LM: training multi-billion parameter language models using model parallelism
why: How the block's matrix products are split across GPUs; the tensor-parallel layout follows the 4 d^2 + 8 d^2 structure of slide 21.

title: ZeRO: memory optimizations toward training trillion parameter models
why: Where training memory goes (weights, gradients, optimizer states) and how to shard it; the accounting behind training at scale.

title: Language models are few-shot learners
why: GPT-3: the 96-layer, 12,288-wide, 175B configuration of slide 22, and the demonstration that scale alone yields in-context learning.

title: Llama 2: open foundation and fine-tuned chat models
why: The 7B/13B/70B configurations cited on slides 22, 25 and 27: RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, GQA at 70B.

title: The Llama 3 herd of models
why: The 8B/70B/405B configurations, 15.6T training tokens, 128k vocabulary, RoPE base 500,000 and GQA with 8 KV heads; the deck's reference for a current model.

title: BERT: pre-training of deep bidirectional transformers for language understanding
why: The encoder-only design of slide 29: bidirectional attention trained to fill in masked tokens.

title: Exploring the limits of transfer learning with a unified text-to-text transformer
why: T5, the encoder-decoder design at scale, with a systematic study of the choices that go into one.

title: LLaMA: open and efficient foundation language models
why: The first Llama: the decoder-only recipe with pre-RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE that most open models have copied since.

title: Mistral 7B
why: A compact current design: GQA, sliding-window attention and a rolling KV cache in a 7B model.

title: Gemma: open models based on Gemini research and technology
why: A 256k-vocabulary decoder-only model with tied embeddings and GeGLU; a useful contrast with Llama's choices.

title: Qwen2.5 technical report
why: A current open family with the same block (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, GQA) and a 152k vocabulary; what 'typical LLM today' on slide 29 looks like in detail.

title: DeepSeek-V3 technical report
why: Where the family goes next: multi-head latent attention compressing the KV cache and a mixture-of-experts MLP; the bridge to the sparsity lecture.

title: The annotated transformer (web page)
why: The 2017 paper interleaved with a working PyTorch implementation, section by section. Secondary source.
